bibliography.abstract: Safety has long been a central concern in transport research, recurring across domains such as road safety, transport planning, and travel behaviour. Existing studies have examined safety through diverse lenses including traffic risk, accident assessment, and experiences of harassment, underscoring that safety is not merely a technical property of transport systems but a socially differentiated and context dependent experience. This paper examines how perceived safety functions as a central component of mobility for older adults in urban Indonesia. For older adults, mobility is not only functional but central to sustaining social participation, access to everyday necessities, and a sense of wellbeing in later life. Yet older adults often face barriers associated with ageing-related health limitations and heightened exposure to unsafe built environments. Drawing on in-depth interviews, go-along interviews, and observations in two Indonesian cities, this study conceptualizes perceived safety as an embodied and relational experience mediated through affect and emotion in everyday mobility. From the perspective of older adults in Indonesia, fear, uncertainty, and emotional strain emerge through repeated encounters with uneven infrastructure, mixed traffic environments, and limited transport services. However, these experiences are not solely characterised by vulnerability; they are also shaped by everyday practices of adaptation, endurance, and tacit acceptance through which older adults continue to navigate and participate in urban life. Both negative and positive affects generate different responses, shaping mobility decisions in iterative ways and producing nuanced perceptions of safety that intersect with financial constraints, health conditions, access to transport modes, and infrastructural conditions. By foregrounding affect and emotion, this paper moves beyond narrow interpretations of safety as accident or crime risk and shows how safety is continuously sensed, negotiated, and reformulated through everyday mobility practices.
bibliography.title: Affective dimensions of perceived safety for older adults’ mobility in urban Indonesia

en.caveats: The findings are based on qualitative interviews and observations in two Indonesian cities, which may limit direct generalizability to regions with different cultural norms of aging or distinct transport infrastructures.
en.what: This study conceptualizes perceived safety as an embodied, affective experience for older adults navigating urban Indonesia. Using in-depth interviews, go-along interviews, and direct observations across two cities, the research documents how older residents experience fear, uncertainty, and emotional strain alongside practices of adaptation and endurance when encountering uneven infrastructure, mixed traffic, and limited transport services.
en.why: It shifts the analytical focus of transport safety away from technical metrics like accident rates or crime statistics toward the continuous, emotional negotiation of the built environment. This provides a framework for understanding how older adults' mobility decisions are shaped by the intersection of physical infrastructure, bodily health, and financial constraints.
